title: Video: Towards An Uncertain Winter For Energy
text:
Video: Towards An Uncertain Winter For Energy

Tom Holland

Gavekal Research

| 30 Jul 2026

With the US-Iran war now five months old, and with no negotiated peace in sight, energy-importing economies must face up to the prospect that supplies of oil and liquefied natural gas from the Persian Gulf will remain severely disrupted as the Northern Hemisphere’s winter approaches. With the European Union’s stores of natural gas already unusually depleted for the time of year, Tom Holland considers the possible consequences for Europe’s economies.

This transcript is auto generated.
Simon Pritchard
Welcome to this weekly Gavekal interview. I'm going to be talking today with Tom Holland, who, among other things for Gavekal, is our energy analyst Tzar. Tom, we're going to be talking about the situation in the Persian Gulf. Now, six weeks after the US and Iran signed that memorandum of understanding on peace, the conflict only seems to be escalating and, perhaps most concerning, spreading. So are there any hopes, would you say, at this juncture for peace, for resumption of normal shipping traffic in that region?
Tom Holland
Well, diplomacy does continue. Both the Pakistanis and the Omanis are trying to find some common ground between Iran and the US. But it has to be said, at this moment, you can't be all that optimistic. There were some hopes for a renewed ceasefire over the weekend. Iran then launched ballistic missiles at a US airbase in Jordan. The US has retaliated. And so, essentially, the fighting there has resumed.
And possibly even more concerning, we're seeing other countries getting dragged into the conflict. So, for example, in the last few days, we saw Saudi Arabia attack Iranian proxies in Iraq. And we've just seen a drone attack on a re-gasification plant, a floating re-gasification facility near Portside in Egypt. So it does appear that the conflict is spreading. And it has to be said that, you know, the efforts at diplomacy do not seem to be gaining much traction.
And part of the problem there is that the intermediaries are talking to the Iranian government, the foreign ministry, the Speaker of the Parliament, whereas really, it's the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that's making the running as far as the conflict is concerned. And there does seem to be considerable distance between these two elements of the Iranian regime. And every time that we see some diplomatic progress, the Revolutionary Guards appear to launch new attacks, whether on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz or on US allies around the region, that then sees the diplomatic efforts break down.
So the upshot is that, to a large extent, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains suspended. We're seeing very little energy traffic, a tanker here and an LNG carrier there. But by and large, shipping is largely suspended.
Simon Pritchard
OK, I guess the question, the immediate question for investors is, what does this mean for global oil and gas supply? And what does it mean for prices?
Tom Holland
Well, if we look back before the beginning of this war, somewhere between 17 million barrels a day and 20 million barrels a day of oil and petroleum products transited through the Strait of Hormuz. Now, that has fallen to, well, really just a few hundred thousand or a million barrels a day at the moment. So we've seen a huge reduction in the tanker traffic transiting through the Strait of Hormuz. Now, countries in the region have tried to compensate as much as they can. Saudi Arabia has been loading around 5 million barrels a day at its Red Sea terminal of Yenbo, up from around 1 million barrels a day before the conflict. Similarly, the United Arab Emirates is pumping as much oil as it can to its terminal of Fujaira on the Gulf of Oman.
But even with these attempts to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, we have seen really a deficit of around about 10 to 11 million barrels a day in global supply caused by the interruption of shipping through the Gulf. So that's a big reduction in global supply.
Now, yes, the global market had been in surplus before the outbreak of this conflict. But still, even allowing for that, we've seen a big reduction of 7 or 8 million barrels a day into deficit as a result of this conflict. And that, of course, is pushing up prices.
Simon Pritchard
OK, but it's not just oil, right? I mean, natural gas supplies have been interrupted as well.
Tom Holland
That's right. Before the conflict, we saw something like a quarter of the world's trade in liquefied natural gas transiting through the Strait of Hormuz, most of that originating in Qatar, which exported something like 10 billion cubic feet a day of gas in LNG form. Now, yes, an LNG carrier from Qatar did transit the Strait in the last day. But essentially, that traffic has ground to a halt. So that means that we've seen a quarter of global LNG trade taken off the market.
Now, again, we have seen other producers attempt to compensate. U.S. exports of liquefied natural gas have been growing faster than anyone expected. If we compare with 2025 last year, the U.S. exported around 15 billion cubic feet a day of LNG. That's now up to around 18 billion cubic feet a day. That's a really bigger increase than anyone expected, given that the rollout times for new export terminals are not terribly flexible.
But that can't compensate for the reduction in supply to the market from Qatar. A 3 billion cubic feet a day increase from the U.S. can't compensate for what amounts almost to 10 billion cubic feet a day lost from Qatari's supply. So, again, we have seen prices rise. If we look at the JKM benchmark in Asia for liquefied natural gas, that's now trading at the equivalent of about $120 a barrel for oil. That's doubled since the outbreak of the conflict. Similarly, if we look at Europe and the TTF benchmark in the Netherlands, it is now trading at around 60 euros per megawatt hour. That's the equivalent of about $110 a barrel for oil. Again, that's more than doubled since the beginning of this conflict. So we are seeing stresses in the LNG market.
Simon Pritchard
Okay. So macroeconomically, in terms of that supply condition, what does that mean for Europe? Because obviously it's been cut off from Russian pipe gas over since the Ukraine conflict.
Tom Holland
That's right. And this is a concern. If we look at Europe's gas stores, what Europe normally does during the summer months is import gas to build up a buffer stock of gas to last it through the winter. And if we look at European gas stocks now, they're less than 60 percent full. And the European gas stocks are at their lowest level for this time of year for the last five years. They're at the very bottom of that five-year range. So this is a concern.
Now, we will see, as a result of this reduction in global supply, increased competition to secure cargoes of LNG. In particular, we'll see European buyers competing with Asian buyers. Now, normally, Europe doesn't actually buy that much gas from the Persian Gulf. It buys around about, in normal times, a billion cubic feet of equivalent of Qatari LNG each day. That's not very much compared to Qatar's normal exports of around 10 billion feet, most of which go to Asia.
However, because we've seen this overall reduction, we do see Asia competing with European buyers for cargoes of US natural gas and, indeed, for cargoes of Russian LNG. And this increased competition basically is going to keep prices elevated going into the European winter.
Now, Europe does have a playbook to deal with this. We did see, the last time, people got very concerned about shortages. In the lead-up and the immediate aftermath of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Europe was short on liquefied natural gas imports, short on piped gas imports, and, of course, short on reserves. We saw this European playbook whereby governments stepped in with fiscal measures to mitigate the impact on households with price gaps, with subsidies. And we also saw, essentially, a reduction in the use of natural gas by energy-intensive industries.
Now, if we do see a cold winter this winter, we might see similar measures initiated again. The problem is, of course, that if you do have subsidies for household energy, if you do have price caps, that, in effect, does not discourage households from using energy. So it doesn't help to reduce energy consumption. And the burden of reduced consumption falls on industry, which, of course, is not great for output. So that increases both fiscal stresses on one hand and weighs on growth on the other hand. So, essentially, if you're in Europe at the moment, you are hoping for a mild winter.
